title: Cross-workload Robustness Notes — May 2025
body:
Purpose and context:

This note captures a focused set of experiments we ran to understand how candidate model variants (v1.8.0, v1.9.0-quant, v2.0-lite) behave across different production-shaped workloads. Goal: surface tradeoffs that aren't obvious from single-benchmark leaderboards (e.g., a model that wins on summarization but regresses on short-dialog safety), and produce a prioritized triage + rollout recommendation.

Summary of procedure:
- Selected four representative workloads: customer-support dialog (turn-based), code-completion (short snippets), search-snippet generation (SEO/FAQ style), and long-form summarization (3–8 paragraph inputs).
- For each workload we used the baseline prompt-set that the product teams run in daily smoke tests (see linked Confluence). We augmented with 50 adversarial edge prompts per workload (see "adversarial-sampler" block below).
- Metrics: head-to-head win-rate (binary prefer A/B by automated preference model), BLEU/ROUGE where applicable, hallucination rate (manual spot checks + heuristic facts), latency P95 (msec on same infra), and per-response token cost estimate.
- Pairwise comparisons: v1.8.0 (prod baseline) vs v1.9.0-quant vs v2.0-lite. Runs executed on same Dedicated pool (g4dn-equivalent) to normalize latency.

Key observations (high level):
1) v1.9.0-quant shows 18% token-cost reduction vs v1.8.0 and maintains parity on code-completion accuracy metrics, but exhibits a statistically significant increase in hallucination rate on long-form summarization (+7 percentage points on sampled failures).
2) v2.0-lite improves conversational safety triggers and out-of-the-box brevity for search-snippet tasks (win-rate +12% vs baseline), but its truncation behavior produces incomplete code suggestions in 11% of code-completion cases (major developer annoyance).
3) Latency P95: v1.9.0-quant = 380ms, v1.8.0 = 430ms, v2.0-lite = 310ms for the short-turn dialog workload. Improvements are consistent with kernel/quant path advantages.

Pairwise win/loss snapshot (automated preference model aggregated over workloads):
- v1.9.0-quant vs v1.8.0: overall win-rate 56% for v1.9.0-quant, but split by workload: code 62%, search 59%, dialog 49%, summarization 40%.
- v2.0-lite vs v1.8.0: overall win-rate 54% for v2.0-lite; code 38%, search 68%, dialog 73%, summarization 45%.

Observed failure modes and example prompts (spot samples):
- Long-form hallucination cluster (v1.9.0-quant): When source text included obscure entity relationships (e.g., "the 2017 Bordeaux donor list"), the quantized variant hallucinated connections across paragraphs that weren't supported by evidence. Example prompt snippet: "Summarize the donor relationships described between paragraphs 4 and 6; are any names repeated with altered titles?" Baseline v1.8.0 answer: "No unsupported links detected." v1.9.0-quant answer: invents an affiliation for "S. Lambert" and asserts an attendance fact.
- Code truncation (v2.0-lite): For multi-function files, the model emits a truncated function body and appends a short "..." without a clear completion token boundary, breaking compile. Example prompt: "Complete the following Python function to validate email addresses across lines using regex and returns canonicalized output." v2.0-lite outputs partial body, missing return statement.
- Dialog brevity mismatch (v1.9.0-quant): In multi-turn clarification scenarios, the quantized variant occasionally drops follow-up clarifying questions, preferring a shorter direct answer and thereby harming downstream task completion quality.

Adversarial-sampler notes:
- We seeded 50 adversarial cases per workload using a mix of: prompt paraphrases from public bug reports, intentionally ambiguous specs, and obfuscated entity tokens. These were crafted to amplify hallucination and truncation errors. Samples are in linked_artifacts PR (see GitHub).

Manual evaluation notes (triage sample size):
- For summarization regression cluster we did a 120-case manual pass: 23 clear hallucinations on v1.9.0-quant vs 9 on v1.8.0. Inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa) ~0.72, acceptable for triage.
- For code truncation we reviewed 80 code completions: v2.0-lite had 9 truncation errors (11%), v1.8.0 had 1 (1%).

Decision considerations and risk matrix:
- Business impact: Code truncation directly impacts developer UX and will generate support tickets quickly; we should bias against models with non-negligible truncation in code endpoints. Summarization hallucination is high-severity for regulated customers (finance/legal) but lower immediate support volume.
- Cost vs quality: v1.9.0-quant reduces token cost significantly; if we can mitigate hallucination via prompt engineering or targeted filters, it remains attractive for search and code (where accuracy held).
- Rollout compatibility: v2.0-lite's safety improvements are desirable for chat endpoints but need a different decode/prefix configuration to avoid truncation in code endpoints.

Immediate recommended actions (short list):
1) Do not promote v1.9.0-quant to default for any summarization/sensitive-regex endpoints until we have a targeted hallucination mitigant. Set as an opt-in variant for search and code (non-critical).
2) Disable v2.0-lite for /code-complete route until we test new decode termination heuristics (increase max_new_tokens and adjust stop-token policy). Run 1,000-case code smoke tests after config change.
3) Run a quick prompt-sensitization pass for v1.9.0-quant on summarization: include explicit evidence-checking instruction and add an automated hallucination detector in the post-process chain (heuristic + small adversarial classifier).
4) Schedule a 2-week follow-up: measure post-mitigation hallucination delta and re-evaluate cost-quality tradeoffs.

Longer-term experiments to run (backlog):
- Kernel-level numeric-stability probes: determine whether hallucination jumps in quant path correlate with specific attention kernel approximations.
- Mixed-precision hybrid run where long-input summarization uses fp16 path and short-turn dialog uses quantized kernels; measure orchestration complexity vs benefit.
- Expand adversarial suite to include 200 real leaked-support transcripts (sanitized) to better approximate production edge cases.

Appendix A — Condensed leaderboard (preferential model aggregated, higher is better):
- v1.9.0-quant: overall 56% vs baseline (wins in code/search; loses on summarization).
- v2.0-lite: overall 54% vs baseline (wins in dialog/search; loses in code).
- v1.8.0 (baseline): retained reasonable balance; higher summarization fidelity than quant variant.

Appendix B — Action items assigned:
- Priya: coordinate prompt-sensitization experiments (due 2025-05-28).
- Ethan: prototype hallucination detector and run on 2k summarization outputs (due 2025-06-04).
- María: run expanded 1k code smoke tests on v2.0-lite with adjusted decoding policy (due 2025-05-30).
- Zoe: add the adversarial seeds to the nightly regression harness and tag runs (ongoing).

Open questions for leadership:
- Tolerance threshold for hallucination delta on summarization endpoints for customers with compliance needs? (proposed: <2% alt-failure rate relative to baseline).
- Appetite to accept code truncation errors during a phased rollout if we gate v2.0-lite to a small cohort?

Notes for reviewers:
- Raw CSV outputs and pairwise matrices uploaded to: https://s3.redwood.ai/experiments/2025-05-crossworkload/ (see README in PR for access).
- The automated preference model has known biases toward brevity; we included manual checks in the two worst-offending clusters to counteract that.

End of note.

Change log:
- 2025-05-12: initial run and draft notes (Priya).
- 2025-05-16: added manual triage counts and expanded adversarial set (Ethan, María).
- 2025-05-20: added rollout recommendations and action items (Priya, Zoe).
